description: We're DuggAI. For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge we built Lunar Window: pick any spot near the Moon's south pole and a date, and see whether a lander gets sunlight for power and can see Earth to radio home. It runs on NASA's LOLA terrain and matches JPL Horizons to within 0.003 degrees. Live at duggai.com/nasa. We build software and data visualizations, and we work online.
summary: Will the Sun reach a lander's solar panels on the Moon, and can it radio Earth? Lunar Window answers both for any landing site and date near the lunar south pole. A live 3D lander camera, ray-traced on your device over NASA LOLA terrain, shows the real Sun and Earth over the real ridges. Compare four sites, walk the terrain, slip the date, see when a lander's battery runs out, find the sunniest spot within 2 km, print a landing plan, or play three short missions. It matches NASA JPL Horizons within 0.0025°, NASA's own LOLA sunlight map at 0.98 correlation, and the Sun's height at all six Apollo landings within 0.02°.
details:
What it does

Lunar Window puts you on the ground at any spot near the Moon's south pole, on any date.

  • The simulator is a full-screen console around a live 3D lander camera over NASA LOLA terrain: the Sun skims the real ridges, shadows move across the craters, and Earth hangs in the sky with its real phase. Drag to look around, scroll to zoom, or switch to a view from above or to four sites at once. You can also walk the lander across the terrain with the W, A, S and D keys or the arrows on screen, and every readout updates as you go.
  • Click "Rises in" or "Sets in" to jump to the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise or Earthset, and Download data saves every time step as a CSV file. Landing plan turns the site and window into one printable page: the view, the numbers, the battery, what a slip does and how the numbers are made. The Map panel also gives the year maps as open data: all 112,992 spots, with the share of the year with the Sun up and with Earth up, in one CSV file.
  • Beside the picture it gives the Sun's angle, whether the lander is in sunlight (power), whether Earth is above the real horizon (direct radio), and how long until each one sets. A timeline underneath shows when the Sun and Earth are up and how the battery holds across the window; drag it, or press play.
  • Each site also gets a lander battery: with a 2 kWh battery, a 150 W load and a 400 W solar panel (all three can be changed), it shows whether the lander lasts the window and, if not, the hour it runs empty. If a sunnier spot lies within 2 km, the simulator marks it and takes you there in one click.
  • Compare up to four sites at once, slip the landing date, see the best days of the next 12 months, or click any point on the south pole map and stand on it.
  • For students and the public there are three short missions on the same model: pick a landing day at Haworth, walk out of Shackleton's shadow, and keep a lander powered and in radio contact for two weeks. Press Land and the window plays out, ending in success or the hour the battery ran empty.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth: Astronomy Engine 2.1.19 (MIT license) plus the IAU 2015 Moon rotation model, computed in the browser. Only the optional live JPL check uses a server. This includes libration: at Haworth, Earth swings from 3.8° below to 10° above the level horizon over 60 days, so the radio link comes and goes.
  • Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_240M. For each of 360 directions the horizon is the steepest angle to the ground. Clicked points get their horizon computed on the spot. The Moon has no air, so there is no refraction: the horizon is the terrain and the curve of the Moon.
  • The 3D view: a ray tracer that runs on the graphics chip (WebGL2). Each pixel's ray is followed through the LOLA heights on the true curved Moon (240 m grid near the pole, 960 m out to 75°S), then a second ray toward the Sun's disk decides light or shadow, with a soft edge from the Sun's real size. Earth is drawn at its true size and phase. Craters smaller than 240 m are drawn for texture only and never hide the Sun or Earth. On a MacBook Pro (Apple M5 Pro) a 1280 × 720 frame takes about 7 ms; on slower computers it draws fewer rays per pixel, then bigger pixels, to stay smooth.
  • Year maps: for every spot within 85.5°S, 720 m apart, the share of a year with the Sun above the local terrain and with Earth in view.
  • Lander battery: an upright panel turned to face the Sun makes its rated power times the cosine of the Sun's angle while the Sun is above the real horizon. The battery starts full, charges and drains against a constant load at each time step (10 to 30 minutes), and never goes above full or below empty.
  • Sunnier spot nearby: the simulator searches the year map within about 2 km of where you stand and points to a spot with at least 5 more points of sunlight.

Worked example

Land at Haworth (an Artemis landing region) on Jan 1, 2027 and the lander gets 72 hours of sunlight in its first 3 days. Land 5 days later and it gets zero. A smooth-Moon calculation misses this kind of thing: at de Gerlache Rim 2 it says the Sun is up 52% of next year, while the real ridges give 80%. On the rim of Shackleton crater the Sun is up 74% of the year; 2.3 km away, on the slope inside, it never rises in the year we modeled. Stand on that slope and the simulator points 2.2 km east to a spot with 41%, and from there 0.7 km south to one with 74%. In the week of Nov 30, 2026, the same lander keeps a full battery at Haworth and de Gerlache Rim 2, but runs empty at the IM-2 site on Dec 1 at 11:20 UTC and at Malapert Massif on Dec 5 at 19:00 UTC.

How we know it is right

  • NASA JPL Horizons: largest gap 0.0025° over 708 checks (3 Artemis landing regions, Sun and Earth, Nov 2026 to May 2027). The page can ask Horizons about any hour live.
  • The LOLA team's own maps (average Sun and Earth visibility at 120 m, method of Mazarico et al. 2011): across all 112,992 of our spots within 85.5°S, our one-year sunlight share correlates with theirs at 0.98 (median difference 1.6 points, 99% of spots within 10 points), Earth visibility at 0.97, and 96.6% of their permanently shadowed spots are dark all year in ours. Their maps count any sliver of the Sun's disk and average many years, so theirs run about 1 point higher.
  • All six Apollo landings: the Sun's height at touchdown matches the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal within 0.02° at every one (Earth within 0.22°; the Journal says its own two calculations differ by up to 0.5°).
  • Chang'e 4: Earth never rises above the horizon there in a full year, which is why a relay satellite was launched before that landing.
  • What moves the answer, measured every hour from Nov 15, 2026 to Nov 15, 2027 at five sites: ignoring terrain changes the year's sunlight by up to 28 points (de Gerlache Rim 2: 52% vs 80%); a 960 m terrain grid instead of 240 m by up to 10 points at rims and peaks (Shackleton rim: 73% vs 83%), which is why we use 240 m near the pole; a 10 m mast instead of 2 m adds up to 12.5 points (Haworth: 61% to 73%); and the 0.0025° gap from JPL moves a sunrise or sunset by about 2 minutes.

Benefits and intended impact

  • The stakes are real. In March 2025 the Athena lander came down in a crater near the south pole, about 400 m from its target (NASA). Its maker said that "with the direction of the sun, the orientation of the solar panels, and extreme cold temperatures in the crater," it did not expect Athena to recharge, and it declared the mission over the next day.
  • People are next. NASA plans Artemis IV for early 2028: two astronauts will spend about a week near the south pole, the first crewed Moon landing in more than 50 years, in one of nine candidate regions. Three of those regions are in Lunar Window.
  • Mission planners can re-check sites and dates in seconds after a schedule change, without reading tables of numbers, and see right away whether a lander's battery would last.
  • Science and engineering teams get one shared picture of power and radio windows. The site list holds landings by the United States, China, India and Japan, so a team from any country can compare its site with the others.
  • Teachers and the public can see why the south pole is so hard: the Sun skims the horizon and a short walk can decide whether a lander has power. Over Houston on December 15 the Sun climbs to 37°; at Haworth it never passes 5° in a whole lunar day.

How it is creative

  • It shows the view from the ground, the way a crew or a lander would see it, instead of tables of angles. You can stand on four sites at once.
  • It turns sunlight into what a mission cares about: hours of battery left, and where to move to get more sun.
  • Every picture is drawn by our code from data, not stock images: the 3D views, the horizon, the year maps and the Shackleton close-up all come from NASA terrain and the real positions of the Sun and Earth.
  • Three missions turn the same model into a game for classrooms: plan a landing, press Land, and watch whether the lander makes it.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript on a static page; WebGL2 and GLSL for the 3D ray tracer; Python for the data build; Node for the checks; Playwright and ffmpeg to record the demo; Microsoft neural text to speech for the narration.

What we considered

  • Accuracy first: we treated our Sun, Earth and sunlight results as predictions and tested them against sources we did not use to build them. JPL Horizons checks the positions, NASA's LOLA maps the sunlight, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal the Sun angles.
  • Easy to read: one idea per screen, labels inside the pictures, works on a phone, and any view can be shared as a link.
  • Limits we state on the page: 240 m terrain misses boulders and small craters; "Earth in view" means direct radio only, no relays; the battery assumes an upright panel that turns to face the Sun and a constant load; dust and temperature are not modeled; sites north of 75°S use a smooth Moon. The next step for choosing an exact landing spot is NASA's finer LOLA south pole maps, down to 5 m (LDEM_875S_5M).

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

SI coding assistants (Claude Code) helped write and test most of the code, ran the checks against JPL Horizons and NASA's LOLA maps, recorded the demo and drafted this text. The idea for Lunar Window is ours. The demo's narration is an SI voice (Microsoft neural text to speech), noted on the video's last frame and in its file metadata. No SI-generated images are used: every picture is rendered by our code from NASA data. We followed the Space Apps guidelines on SI: we used it as a tool to accelerate innovation and creativity for our solution, and we acknowledge where it was used, here and in the project's code and metadata.
